Scope. I read all fourteen named files of the host engine under /Users/acoerduek/Documents/workspace/cuopt-wt/gpu-presolve/gpu_presolve (include/gprs/state.hpp, numerics.hpp, rules.hpp, presolve.hpp, postsolve.hpp, assert.hpp; src/state_build.cpp, state_ops.cpp, state_storage.cpp, rules_propagation.cpp, rules_bounds.cpp, rules_rows.cpp, presolve.cpp, hash.cpp), plus src/postsolve.cpp lines 1-110, DESIGN.md sections 0-4, 6, 12, 13, and microbench/sweeps.cu lines 196-470 to compare the Stage 0 kernels with the host summation order. Nothing was built or run. Statements marked "inferred" are my conclusions, the rest is read from the code.

State layout. state_t (state.hpp:198-421) is entirely std::vector with the default allocator. The matrix is two line_store_t (CSR and CSC, state.hpp:62-75): per line start (int64), used, capacity, size (int32); per slot index (int32, -1 is a tombstone), value (double), twin (int64 slot in the other store). Rows carry row_lower, row_upper, row_alive (uint8), row_free_size (live entries in live columns), row_version (uint32). Columns carry col_lower, col_upper (the explicit bounds), cost, col_type, col_status (live / fixed / removed), down_locks, up_locks, and the implied bounds of continuous columns as six separate arrays (value, source row, row version per side). Fixed columns keep their entries in the rows as constant terms until rebuild. Each of the two activities (activity_t, state.hpp:86-95) is six arrays per row: hi, lo (double), inf_count (int32, exact), inf_slot (int64, sum of the host CSR slots of the infinite terms), max_term (double), updates (uint32). The pair (hi, lo) is not normalised: hi can be 0 while lo holds the value (state.hpp:84-85). Frontier marks are frontier_set_t (state.hpp:109-151): a uint8 pending mask per index and one ordered std::vector<int32_t> per consumer; six row lists (row_rules, propagation, tightening, doubleton, parallel_rows, compaction) and two column lists (dual_fixing, compaction). There is no list of changed columns and no list of "changed since the device last saw it". Counters: live_rows, live_cols, live_nnz, fixed_nnz, bound_changes, side_changes, coefficient_changes (all hashed), slot_visits (not hashed), objective_offset as a compensated pair.

Summation order. numerics.hpp:139-155 defines the one order for an activity summed from scratch: the n live entries of a row (entries of fixed columns included, tombstones skipped) in storage order, entry k to lane k mod activity_lanes(n); lanes = smallest power of two with 2*lanes >= n up to 64 entries, 256 above; each lane adds with dd_add_product in order; lanes merged by lane[l] = dd_add(lane[l], lane[l+off]) for off = lanes/2 ... 1. state_t::fold_row_activity (state_build.cpp:339-346) is the only place an activity is summed. After a fold the stored side is hi, lo, inf_count, inf_slot, max_term = largest |a*bound| of the finite terms, updates = number of finite terms (state_build.cpp:216-224).

Bound change. tighten_lower / tighten_upper (rules_bounds.cpp:15-49) round an integer bound (ceil(l - feas), floor(u + feas)), do nothing if not tighter, return infeasible if the bound crosses the opposite one by more than feas (or is the wrong infinity), fix the column at the opposite bound when they meet, else call set_col_lower / set_col_upper. set_col_bound (state_ops.cpp:180-196) walks the column's CSC in storage order and, per row, removes the old term and adds the new one in the one activity that holds that bound (two terms, never a*(new-old); an infinite term changes inf_count and inf_slot instead), bumps max_term and updates, pushes the row on the row_rules, propagation and tightening lists, and recomputes the row when a side is stale (updates >= 2*size and updates*u^2*max_term > 0.1*feas). It increments bound_changes. It does not change row_version, locks or any column list, and it writes no postsolve record. fix_col (state_ops.cpp:259-292) sets both bounds, status fixed, replaces the terms on the sides whose bound moved, decrements row_free_size of each row, pushes the rows with row_event::entries (adds the doubleton and parallel_rows lists), decrements live_cols, adds csc.size to fixed_nnz, adds cost*value to objective_offset (compensated, so the order of fixings changes its bits). fix_column (rules_bounds.cpp:51-58) adds the only postsolve record a bound change can produce: push_fixed_col(col, value) (postsolve.cpp:93-102), appended in application order. An implied bound of a continuous column is three array writes (state_ops.cpp:315-329) and no postsolve record.

Propagation rule (rules_propagation.cpp). run (138-170) takes the propagation list and visits rows in list order, repeating until the list stays empty or the budget stops (tested between rows; unvisited live rows are pushed back, stopped = true). Per row the upper side with the minimum activity comes first, then the lower side with the maximum activity (163). propagate_side (111-134): skip if the side is infinite or |side|*1e-14 > feas; inf_count > 1 gives nothing; inf_count == 1 gives one candidate, the entry at inf_slot if its column is live; inf_count == 0 scans the row in storage order over live entries of live columns. candidate (51-73): rest = activity minus the column's own term (dd_sub_product, updates+1) when there is no infinite term; no candidate if activity_error(updates, max_term) > 0.1*feas*|a|; bound = dd_residual(side, rest)/a; dropped if not finite. Integer column (82-92): the bound is moved outward by 4*u*|bound|, then tighten_* rounds and applies it at once (Gauss-Seidel: later rows and the lower side of the same row see it). Continuous column (94-107): the explicit bound is not touched; the bound is recorded when it beats the valid record by more than implied_bound_step*feas (1000*1e-6), whatever the explicit bound is. Within one side of one row the activity used is not changed by that side's own candidates (comment at 46-50), so candidates of one row side from one snapshot equal the host's sequential result for that side (inferred from that comment and fix_col's "if side != value" test). make_explicit (172-192) runs once at the end.

Driver (presolve.cpp). presolve (314-328) builds postsolve and state, runs start_step (62-95), then rounds (246-259): cascade (207-221: row_rules, propagation, tightening, dual_fixing per pass, compact_sparse_lines after each pass, at most 100 passes, stop when a call stopped on budget or nothing is pending), end_phase, parallel_rows, end_phase, doubleton, end_phase, until a round has no finding or 20 rounds. call (177-195) skips a family that is off or has an empty list, tests the time limit, makes the budget from the current state (presolve.hpp:69-76; propagation 16 passes, stall 2 passes, floor 100,000), runs it and books statistics. end_phase (232-244) rebuilds when dead_fraction > 0.25 or fixed_nnz > 0.25*live_nnz, else compacts; record_phase (223-230) asserts consistency_error().empty() and, with phase_hashes, hashes state and postsolve. Statuses: infeasible from start_step (267), a family's outcome (269, 276), final_status (301-309: limit, unchanged, reduced_to_empty, reduced). There is no engine choice, no device option and no device statistics anywhere in options_t, result_t or the driver.

Hash (hash.cpp). state_hash (139-178) covers tolerances, both stores with their layout (start, used, capacity, size, slot count, index of every used slot, value and twin of live slots), sides, row_alive, row_free_size, row_version, both activities with all six arrays, bounds, cost, type, status, locks, the six implied-bound arrays, objective_offset, the seven counters and every list in its order. Not hashed: slot_visits, lane_scratch, pending masks, value and twin of tombstones. postsolve_hash covers the records in order.

What a device propagation round reads: the CSR entries per row in storage order (and the CSC, or an equivalent, to find the rows of a changed column), row sides, row_alive, column bounds, col_type, col_status, the five tolerances feasibility, infinite_term, activity_error_share, implied_bound_step, side_error, the stored activities of rows it does not recompute (including updates and max_term for the guard and the unnormalised lo), the propagation list as its starting frontier, and, if it records implied bounds itself, the implied arrays with row_alive and row_version for validity. What it writes (directly or through the hand-back): explicit bounds of integer columns; col_status fixed; the six activity arrays of every row with a changed column; implied-bound records of continuous columns; row_free_size; the row lists; live_cols, fixed_nnz, bound_changes; objective_offset; fixed_col postsolve records; the budget and rule_result_t. It never touches matrix entries or layout, twins, sides, row_alive, row_version, locks, cost, live_rows, live_nnz, side_changes, coefficient_changes, the compaction lists or the column lists.

Invariants a hand-back must restore are those of state_t::consistency_error (state_storage.cpp:637-820) plus the rule contract (rules.hpp:49-73); they are listed in the constraints. The consistency check accepts any activity within a proven error bound of the fold, so it does not by itself enforce the bit equality that decision 5 requires.

A fold result handed to the host is six values per side, not two: hi, lo, the exact inf_count, inf_slot as the sum of host CSR slots of the infinite terms, max_term = largest |a*bound| over finite terms, updates = number of finite terms (= csr.size[row] - inf_count). max_term is a max reduction and inf_slot an integer sum, so both are order-free; inf_slot can be produced as inf_count * host row start + sum of in-row positions, the same shift rebuild applies (state_storage.cpp:135-137).

The host inf_count is int32 and must be exact at hand-back (check_activity compares it with the fold). A device uint16 count that saturates cannot be handed back; such a row needs a host recount (fold) or an exact integer reduction at hand-back.

The host accumulator pair is not normalised (state.hpp:84-85). A device candidate may not be computed from hi alone on a row whose accumulators came from host updates unless lo is known to be zero or the row was refolded on the device.

A device round must apply the same candidate rule as rules_propagation.cpp: side guard (finite side, |side|*side_error <= feasibility), 0 / 1 / more infinite terms, residual first with the own term removed by dd_sub_product, error guard activity_error(updates(+1), max_term) <= activity_error_share*feasibility*|a|, finite quotient, integer candidates moved outward by 4*u*|bound| then rounded by ceil(l - feas) / floor(u + feas), infeasible when the new bounds cross by more than feasibility, fixed when they meet. Candidates only for live columns of live rows.

Explicit bounds of continuous columns must not be changed by a device propagation round. Continuous candidates go to the implied-bound record only (value, source row, row_version of that row), improving the valid record by more than implied_bound_step*feasibility; no record on an integer column; a record needs a live source row.

Every column the device fixes needs, on the host and in one fixed order: status fixed with lower == upper == an integral finite value, one postsolve fixed_col record (order is hashed), objective_offset += cost*value by dd_add_product (the order changes its bits), --live_cols, fixed_nnz += csc.size[col], --row_free_size for each of its rows, and those rows pushed with row_event::entries.

Every row with a changed column must be pushed with row_event::activity (row_rules, propagation, tightening lists) and must hold activities that pass check_activity and are not stale; bound_changes must grow by one per bound value that moved. The order of the lists is hashed and decides the order in which the host families visit rows afterwards, so the hand-back needs one defined order (for example ascending changed column then CSC storage order, which is what a replay through the host operations gives, or ascending row index).

A hand-back must leave unchanged: both stores and their layout, twins, row sides, row_alive, row_version, locks, cost, col_type, live_rows, live_nnz, side_changes, coefficient_changes, the compaction lists and both column lists. Deleted rows must keep all six activity values at zero.

State invariants assumed by every host family after a hand-back (rules.hpp:49-73, presolve.hpp:166-173): lower <= upper on every live row and column, lower < upper on every live column, integral bounds on integer columns, a postsolve record for every removed column, and state_t::consistency_error() empty. record_phase asserts the latter after every phase and rebuild asserts it at its end, so the host arrays must be complete and current whenever end_phase runs.
With outcome infeasible the state is not used again (rules.hpp:65-66), so a device round that finds infeasibility needs no hand-back; the status comes from the round's outcome.

Budget, findings and the stopped flag of a device round must be computed from counts that are the same on every machine (work units of rules.hpp:20-22), because budget.stop() decides how far propagation goes and a stopped call ends the cascade pass loop (presolve.cpp:218). An unfinished round must leave its unprocessed rows on the propagation list.

The device copy of the matrix is tied to host slots only through inf_slot and through the entry order of each row. compact_sparse_lines (after every cascade pass) and rebuild change host slots; move_entry (doubleton) reorders CSC columns and moves them to the end of the store. A device mirror must be refreshed or re-derived after these, and a device rebuild that is to equal the host rebuild must keep each line's entry order (also in the CSC), sum the fixed terms of a row sequentially in storage order, shift the sides by dd_residual, recompute only rows that lost a slot and shift inf_slot of the others.

state_t is std::vector throughout and the CSC grows by resize (state_ops.cpp:160-162); lists grow by push_back. A presolve-owned memory resource with host_access / release, and managed memory read in place on Grace Hopper, cannot be put under the current types without changing state.hpp (owned by part A) or keeping separate device arrays with copies.

The device code cannot call the inline functions of numerics.hpp as they are (no device annotations); it needs either annotations in that shared header or a copy whose bits are tested against the host (fold, dd_residual, two_prod with one explicit fma, contraction off in the CUDA build as well).

The driver has no place for an engine choice yet. A device round has to enter either inside call(rule::propagation) or as a new step of cascade(); options_t needs the thresholds and a force switch for tests, result_t needs statistics, and rule::count == 6 sizes three arrays and is tied to the row list numbering by a static_assert (presolve.cpp:41-46).
open_questions: Hand-back method. Either the device returns only the net bound changes and the host replays them through tighten_lower / tighten_upper in a fixed order (every invariant, list, counter, record and the offset follow by construction; cost is the CSC length of the changed columns; activities are then incremental host bits and the device folds are discarded), or the device's folded accumulators are written into the host arrays as bits, as DESIGN.md 2.2 words it (needs a new state_t member that does the bookkeeping without the activity arithmetic, and a defined list order). Which one, and is the choice the same on both memory paths?

Rows above 8,192 entries and the 65 to 8,192 block: keep the order of numerics.hpp (one block striding the whole row with 256 lanes and the fixed tree) or redefine the order with a chunk level for both engines? The second changes fold_heavy_row and the host hashes on matrices with such rows.

How are host changes carried to the device on x86? The host keeps no list of columns whose bounds or status changed and no list of rows whose activities, sides or entries changed since a given point; the row lists are consumed by the host families. Two spare bits exist in the row pending mask and six in the column mask, but new lists change state_hash, and set_col_bound and fix_col push no column list today.

Is the state rebuilt before the device matrix is built after the first cascade? end_phase rebuilds only by the two fractions; without a rebuild the rows still hold tombstones and entries of fixed columns, which the device must then mirror to get the same fold bits.

Continuous columns on the device: the host records sequentially (each record must beat the previous by the step, in row list order), a device round would take the best candidate per column and side with its source row. Which rule defines the record on the device, what breaks ties between rows, and does the device write the record or does the host apply it from the returned candidates (the host would then also do the validity test with row_alive and row_version)?

The planned test 'integer-only models run to an empty frontier reach the same bounds on both engines' can fail without a bug: the error guard depends on updates and max_term, which grow with incremental host updates and are reset by a device fold, so one engine can drop a candidate the other accepts (small |a| with terms near 1e20). Is the test restricted to models where the guard cannot fire, or is the guard made independent of history?

Counts of infinite terms: is the device array uint16 with saturation and a host recount for saturated rows, and is the Stage 0 packing (15-bit count plus a flag for lo != 0) kept? The host needs the exact int32 and inf_slot for every live row at hand-back.

What is the work of a device round in budget units (entries of the frontier rows plus 8 per row, plus the columns changed?), how are findings counted so that the stall limit behaves as on the host, and are the device rounds booked under rule::propagation or as their own statistics entry?

Does a device propagation call run to an empty frontier like the host call (several rounds inside one call), or one round per call with the host deciding between rounds? This fixes where the hand-back threshold of DESIGN.md 2.1 is tested.

Should the device rebuild be required to equal the host rebuild bit for bit (state_hash equality as the test)? The stable radix sort transpose gives columns in row order, which differs from the host's kept column order once move_entry has run; the compaction path keeps it.

May numerics.hpp and state.hpp, which presolve.hpp lists as fixed interfaces of parts shared and A, be edited for device annotations, an allocator or memory-resource parameter and a hand-back entry point, or must the device engine stay outside them?

With phase_hashes on and no pinned mirror above the size threshold, state_hash and consistency_error read every host array at each phase end. Is the full state copied back for those builds, or is a device-side hash defined that equals state_hash?

readers.summary:
What was read. In full: /Users/acoerduek/Documents/workspace/cuopt-wt/gpu-presolve/gpu_presolve/microbench/sweeps.cu (2,680 lines), sweeps_cpu.cpp, fixed_costs.cu, README_sweeps.md, README_fixed_costs.md and CMakeLists.txt in the same directory; /Users/acoerduek/Documents/workspace/cuopt-wt/gpu-presolve/gpu_presolve/results/stage0/STAGE0_REPORT.md; DESIGN.md sections 0 to 3, 12 and 13; and the checked analysis record results/stage0/analysis/cost_model_findings.json (engine part, and the summary and recommendations of the kernel part). To see what the device kernels have to match, I also read the parts of the Stage 1a host engine that define an activity and a candidate: include/gprs/numerics.hpp, include/gprs/state.hpp (activity_t), src/state_build.cpp, src/rules_propagation.cpp and tests/test_state_fold.cpp. Nothing was built or run. One statement below about the inside of cub::BlockReduce is from memory and is marked as such.

What exists. sweeps.cu is one benchmark program with templated kernels. It times 28 activity variants, 10 candidate variants, one frontier path, four ways to rebuild the CSC and a one-thread CPU reference. fixed_costs.cu times launches, read-backs, library primitives, copies, allocations, dirty lists, a row gather and managed memory. Neither is engine code: there is no state object, no loop over rounds, no application of a bound, and every failure is an abort.

Lane groups (sweeps.cu lines 170-176, 328-386, 1188-1235). Rows are put into classes by length: 0-2, 3-4, 5-8, 9-16, 17-32, 33-64 (the six classes that one kernel launch covers), 65-8,192 (one 256-thread block per row) and above 8,192 (one block per chunk of 8,192 entries, then one block per row over the chunk results). The host sorts the rows by class with a stable counting sort and writes a second copy of the CSR in that order. A row of class c is folded by 2^c adjacent lanes of a warp, so 32 >> c rows share a warp and every class starts at a new warp. Lane s of a group reads the entries at positions s, s + 2^c of the row, so a lane holds at most two entries. The lanes are combined by __shfl_down_sync with offsets 2^c / 2, ..., 2, 1, and lane 0 of the group writes the result. The tree therefore depends only on the row's class and the position of each entry in the row.

Compensated sums and counts (lines 200-309, 388-414). Every thread keeps (hi, lo, count) per side. A term with |a * bound| above 1e20, or not finite, raises the local count and is not summed. Otherwise the product error comes from one explicit fma and the addition error from a two-sum, both added to lo; two partial sums are merged by a two-sum of the hi parts. In block and chunk kernels the partial sums are reduced by cub::BlockReduce. The count of infinite terms is done in two ways: reduced like the sums (carried through the shuffles, or a second cub::BlockReduce pair), or counted in the scan and added with one integer atomic on a shared-memory counter only when the local count is nonzero. The output is either one {double sum, double count} pair per side, or a double array plus a uint16_t array per side; lo always goes to a separate array. In the uint16_t layout bit 15 means "lo is not zero" and the count saturates at 32,767.

Candidate kernel (lines 471-647). It runs per column over the CSC. For every entry it reads the row's side; if the side is finite it reads the count, then the sum only when the count is at most one, forms the residual activity minus a * own bound in compensated arithmetic, and divides (side - residual) by a. With one infinite term only the column whose own term is infinite gets a candidate. The column keeps the largest lower and smallest upper candidate, rounds them for integer columns with 1e-6, and stores them. It does not compare with the current bound, apply anything, evaluate an error guard, detect infeasibility or mark anything as changed. Columns are scheduled like rows: lane groups through a list sorted by class (no second copy of the CSC), or one thread per column up to 64 entries, with blocks and chunks above.

Frontier kernel of that version (lines 2121-2192). The frontier is a ready-made uint8_t flag array of random rows. Two cub::DeviceSelect::Flagged calls make a list of the flagged rows up to 64 entries and a list of those from 65 to 8,192; the two counts are copied to the host with a blocking copy; then the rows up to 64 are computed with one thread per row and the others with one block per row; chunk kernels are launched over all long rows and test the flag. Only activities are computed; there is no frontier-restricted candidate kernel. The plan asks for a new kernel for two reasons that the report gives: lane groups won the full sweep (0.69 times one thread per row up to 64), and their sums differ in bits from one thread over the row on 9 of 32 matrices, so a full sweep with lane groups next to this frontier kernel would give one row two summation orders (decision 5 forbids that); and this path was slower than recomputing all rows with lane groups on all 16 matrices below 5e5 nonzeros, because the compaction alone costs 34 to 67 microseconds.

Rebuild (lines 649-768, 1326-1458, 2306-2421). 20% of the rows and 20% of the columns are flagged dead. The CSR is compacted by scans of the flags, a keep flag per entry, a scan and a scatter. The CSC is then built by a stable cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs on (column, position), by a histogram and scatter with integer atomics (order depends on timing) with or without a segmented sort, or by compacting the old CSC. Buffers and CUB temporary storage are allocated before the timed part. Result: radix sort 467 microseconds + 0.279 ns per nonzero, faster than scatter plus segmented sort on 24 of 32; compaction of the old CSC 0.70 times that. Re-binning by length, entry tombstones and the carry-over of state arrays were not part of it.

Where the provisional thresholds come from. All are in report section 6 and cost_model_findings.json. Full sweep on the GPU from 32,000 nonzeros: extrapolated from the 32 matrices (smallest 71,477 nonzeros), per-matrix crossover 8,954 to 55,553, median 18,453, computed with the version 3 kernel pair, not with lane groups. Frontier on the GPU from nonzeros + 8 * rows >= 20,000 work units: from a GPU frontier pass of 56 to 141 microseconds and a host cost of about 10 ns per frontier nonzero warm; best single threshold 9,514 to 53,817 depending on the reading; the whole GPU step is modelled as twice its activity part. Frontier-restricted sweep only from about 1e6 nonzeros and frontiers of at most 1% of the rows: measured with the old frontier kernel. Rebuild on the GPU from 100,000 nonzeros: fitted crossover 86,442 against one CPU thread at 5.68 ns per nonzero. Pinned mirror below 64 MiB: a placeholder.

What I found in the host engine that changes what is reusable. The host engine has since fixed the summation order of an activity "the same in every engine" (numerics.hpp lines 139-155): the live entries of a row in storage order are dealt to lanes (entry k to lane k mod lanes), with 1 to 32 lanes up to 64 entries and 256 lanes above, merged with offsets lanes/2, ..., 1. By reading, this is exactly the benchmark's lane-group kernel for rows up to 64 entries, including the arithmetic. It is not what the benchmark computes above 64 entries: the block kernel deals entries to 256 threads in the same way but merges with cub::BlockReduce, and the chunk kernels cut a long row into pieces of 8,192, which cannot give the bits of 256 lanes that each run over the whole row. The host also stores more per side than the benchmark computes (the slot of the single infinite entry, the largest term, the update count; int32 counts), and its propagation rule has tests the benchmark kernel lacks (error guard, side size, outward move before integer rounding, implied-bound records for continuous columns instead of tightening).

Reusable: the term and merge arithmetic, the light-row kernel and its plan, the column lane-group kernel with its list argument, the entry walk that is independent of row lengths, CSR compaction, the radix-sort transpose, the chunk bookkeeping, and the checks as a pattern. Not to be copied: everything listed under facts as scaffolding.
facts: Activity variants are named scheduling/layout/count/arithmetic and enumerated in /Users/acoerduek/Documents/workspace/cuopt-wt/gpu-presolve/gpu_presolve/microbench/sweeps.cu:2007-2016: scheduling T, B, H, C; layout P (paired) or S (split); count R (reduced) or A (atomic); arithmetic plain or comp. T has no R variant, so there are 4 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 28 variants. The meaning of the letters is in /Users/acoerduek/Documents/workspace/cuopt-wt/gpu-presolve/gpu_presolve/microbench/README_sweeps.md:64-75.

Scheduling T (sweeps.cu:1770-1773): act_light_kernel with a one-class plan over the CSR as given, one thread per row whatever its length. Scheduling C (sweeps.cu:1788): act_block_kernel with one 256-thread block per row over the CSR as given; the report calls it the benchmark's rendering of cuOpt's scheme, cuOpt's own kernel was not run (STAGE0_REPORT.md:51-55).

Scheduling B (sweeps.cu:1774-1780): act_light_kernel with the six-class plan on the sorted copy of the CSR (lane groups), then act_block_kernel for rows of 65 to 8,192 entries, then act_chunk_kernel and act_chunk_finalize_kernel for longer rows. Scheduling H (sweeps.cu:1781-1787): the same above 64 entries, and a one-class plan (one thread per row) up to 64.

Length classes are computed in sweeps.cu:1188-1194 (length_class): up to 2 entries class 0, then 63 - clz(len - 1), so 3-4, 5-8, 9-16, 17-32, 33-64 are classes 1 to 5; above 64 the block class, above 8,192 the chunk class. Constants are at sweeps.cu:99-105 (block of 256 threads, 64, 8,192, six light classes).

Rows are ordered by class on the host by a stable counting sort (classify, sweeps.cu:1203-1222) and copied into a second CSR in that order (make_binned, sweeps.cu:1277-1295). The plan gives every class its own range of warps, with 32 >> c rows per warp (binned_plan, sweeps.cu:1224-1235).

A thread finds its row in light_slot (sweeps.cu:328-342): warp index from block and thread index, class by a linear search over at most six warp boundaries, group size g = 1 << c, lane within the group sub = lane & (g - 1), row k = row_begin[c] + (warp - warp_begin[c]) * (32 >> c) + (lane >> c).

In act_light_kernel (sweeps.cu:346-386) lane sub scans the entries start + sub, start + sub + g, ... of its row (line 360), so at most two entries per lane. The lanes are merged by __shfl_down_sync with offsets g/2, ..., 1 (lines 376-383, shfl_merge at 242-249) and the thread with sub == 0 stores the row (line 385). All 32 lanes take part in every shuffle; an invalid group holds zeros.

Compensated term (add_term, sweeps.cu:200-217): p = a * b; if not |p| <= 1e20 the local count is raised and nothing is summed; else pe = fma(a, b, -p), t = hi + p, z = t - hi, lo += ((hi - (t - z)) + (p - z)) + pe, hi = t. Merge of two partial sums (dd_add, sweeps.cu:219-224): two-sum of the hi parts, lo = (a.lo + b.lo) + error. The pair is not normalised.

In block and chunk kernels the partial sums of the 256 threads are reduced by cub::BlockReduce, with the two-sum operator for compensated sums (block_reduce_sums, sweeps.cu:251-270; block_fold, sweeps.cu:388-414). Thread t scans entries beg + t, beg + t + 256, ... (line 401).

Count of infinite terms in the lane-group kernel (sweeps.cu:362-383): variant A zeroes two shared-memory ints per group, each lane does one atomicAdd only if its local count is nonzero, between two __syncwarp calls; variant R carries the count through the same shuffles as the sums. Rows of class 0 need neither.

Count of infinite terms in block kernels (sweeps.cu:393-413): variant A uses two shared ints per block and one atomicAdd per thread with a nonzero local count; variant R runs a second cub::BlockReduce pair (block_reduce_counts, sweeps.cu:272-283), on doubles in the paired layout and on ints in the split layout (line 425). act_chunk_finalize_kernel always reduces the chunk counts with a block reduction (sweeps.cu:467), in every variant.

Output layouts (store, sweeps.cu:290-309): paired writes pair_t{sum, (double)count} per side; split writes a double hi array and a uint16_t count array per side. pack_count (sweeps.cu:285-288) saturates the count at 32,767 and sets bit 15 when lo is not zero. lo is always a separate array.

Rows above 8,192 entries (sweeps.cu:433-469, chunks_t at 1249-1275): one block per chunk of 8,192 entries writes a part_t (four doubles, two ints); a second kernel with one block per row merges the parts of the row. The chunk lists are built on the host with push_back loops.

Candidate kernel core (sweeps.cu:471-564): load_side reads the count first and returns without a candidate when it is above one; the sum is read only then; lo is read always (paired, or split 'always') or only when bit 15 is set (split 'gated'). residual_candidate forms activity - a * own bound and (side - residual) / a in compensated arithmetic; with one infinite term only the column whose own term is infinite gets a candidate (line 507). store_candidate rounds integer columns with ceil(lb - 1e-6) and floor(ub + 1e-6) and writes cand_lb[j], cand_ub[j].

Candidate scheduling (sweeps.cu:566-647, 811-835): cand_light_kernel takes a list of columns sorted by class ('order') and the same light plan as the rows, with min/max over the lanes by shuffles; cand_block_kernel uses one block per column and cub::BlockReduce with min and max; cand_chunk_kernel and cand_chunk_finalize_kernel handle columns above 8,192. The ten variants are listed at sweeps.cu:1688-1694: B or H scheduling times P/plain, S/plain, P/comp, S/comp/gated, S/comp/always.

README_sweeps.md:110 states that the candidate kernel evaluates no error guard and suppresses no candidate; README_sweeps.md:214-215 lists as limits that there is no frontier-restricted candidate kernel on the device and that the error guard of DESIGN.md 2.4 is not modelled.

Frontier path (sweeps.cu:2149-2192): two cub::DeviceSelect::Flagged calls over a uint8_t flag array in binned order (rows up to 64, rows of 65 to 8,192), a blocking cudaMemcpy of the two counts (lines 2173-2174), then act_light_kernel with single_class_plan over the first list (one thread per row, line 2183) and act_block_kernel over the second, both split layout with atomic counts; chunk kernels run over all long rows and test the flag (line 2191, test at sweeps.cu:440 and 456). The frontiers are random rows (make_frontiers, sweeps.cu:2121-2147).

act_light_kernel already takes a row list and any light plan as arguments (sweeps.cu:346-352, 359). The frontier path only passes a one-class plan. Since the compacted list keeps the binned order, it is already sorted by class; a plan built from the per-class counts of the list would run the same lane groups on frontier rows. This is my inference from the code, not something the benchmark does.

Measured for that frontier path (cost_model_findings.json, engine, confirmed claims): compaction alone 33.6 to 66.6 microseconds; compaction plus the kernels 56.1 to 141 microseconds at 0.01% of the rows (median 81.9) and 67.5 to 363 at 10%. Below 5e5 nonzeros it is slower than a full lane-group sweep at every frontier size on all 16 matrices; from 1e6 nonzeros it wins at 1% of the rows and below (kernels part, added recommendation; STAGE0_REPORT.md:329-331).

STAGE0_REPORT.md:387-394 (decision 5): lane groups differ in bits from a single thread over the row on 9 of 32 matrices (hi + lo as one double is equal on all 32); the version 3 scheme differs on 5 through its block trees. The fallback scheme (one thread per row up to 64, blocks above, for full and frontier sweeps) costs 1.45 times the lane-group activity kernel, a median of 42 microseconds more per sweep. DESIGN.md:264-269 enters this.

Kernel results in STAGE0_REPORT.md:299-309: lane groups take 0.69 times one thread per row up to 64, 0.19 times one block per row and 0.10 times one thread per row (geometric mean, compensated); compensated sums cost 39% in the activity kernel and 14% of a sweep; in the one-block-per-row scheme the atomic count takes 0.71 (plain) and 0.84 (compensated) times a second block reduction; inside lane groups the two count methods are equal (0.97 and 1.00) and the atomic one is 9% to 11% slower on supportcase42; paired against split arrays and gating are not decided (two variants doing identical work differ by up to 12%).

Rebuild code: compact (sweeps.cu:1366-1398) does two exclusive scans of the alive flags, a keep flag per entry through walk_entries_kernel, a scan of the keep flags into 32-bit positions, compact_scatter_kernel, compact_start_kernel and three blocking copies of the totals. transpose_radix (sweeps.cu:1407-1422) records row and position per entry, builds column offsets by histogram_kernel (integer atomics) and a scan, sorts (column, position) with cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs over only the bits the column count needs, and gathers.

walk_entries_kernel (sweeps.cu:663-683): each thread owns 32 consecutive entries, finds its row by binary search over the offsets and walks them, so the cost does not depend on the row length distribution. It is used for the keep flags, the row expansion and the scatter.

transpose_scatter (sweeps.cu:1426-1458) scatters with one atomicAdd per entry on a per-column cursor; the order inside a column depends on thread timing unless cub::DeviceSegmentedSort::SortPairs follows. Compaction of the old CSC is compact() with rows and columns swapped (sweeps.cu:2342-2344) and only works when entries were only deleted.

Rebuild benchmark set-up (sweeps.cu:2306-2421; README_sweeps.md:142-163): 20% of the rows and 20% of the columns dead by independent draws; scratch arrays and CUB temporary storage allocated before timing; every row of the table divided by the nonzeros of the original matrix; results compared with a host rebuild. Positions are 32-bit, so fewer than 2^31 nonzeros (README_sweeps.md:212-213).

Rebuild results (STAGE0_REPORT.md:309; cost_model_findings.json): compact CSR plus radix sort 467 microseconds + 0.279 ns per nonzero; faster than scatter plus segmented sort on 24 of 32 totals; compaction of the old CSC 343 microseconds + 0.170 ns per nonzero (0.70 times); one CPU thread (5.68 ns per nonzero) is faster on the matrices up to about 100,000 nonzeros, fitted crossover 86,442 (96,624 from band A). Re-binning by length was not timed.

Threshold 'full sweep on the GPU from 32,000 nonzeros' (STAGE0_REPORT.md:340, DESIGN.md:172): the GPU is cheaper on all 32 matrices from 71,477 nonzeros up; the crossover is extrapolated, 3,235 to 21,960 from the fits and 8,954 to 55,553 per matrix (median 18,453) with the kernel pair H/S/A/comp plus the faster of H/S/comp/gated and B/S/comp/gated, fitted as 126 microseconds + 0.145 ns per nonzero. That pair is the version 3 scheme, not lane groups.

Threshold 'frontier on the GPU from nonzeros + 8 * rows >= 20,000 units' (STAGE0_REPORT.md:341, DESIGN.md:173): unit 10 ns, the warm host cost per frontier nonzero; row weight from the fitted host cost (88.3 ns per row + 8.41 ns per nonzero cold, 19.3 + 4.92 warm); activity-only crossover median 9,940 frontier nonzeros cold and 23,866 warm; best single threshold 9,514 to 53,817 depending on the reading; the GPU step is modelled as twice its activity part because no frontier candidate kernel exists.

Threshold 'frontier-restricted GPU sweep only from about 1e6 nonzeros and frontiers of at most 1% of the rows' (STAGE0_REPORT.md:342, DESIGN.md:174) is an in-sample boundary measured with the old frontier kernel. 'Rebuild on the GPU from 100,000 nonzeros' (line 343) is the fitted crossover without hand-over. 'Pinned mirror below 64 MiB' (line 344) is a placeholder, not derived.

constraints_for_design: The summation order is already fixed by the host engine (numerics.hpp:139-155) and the device kernels have to produce its bits. For rows up to 64 entries the benchmark's lane-group kernel does this by construction, as far as reading shows: same dealing of entries to lanes, same term arithmetic, same merge offsets. This holds only when the row has no tombstone and the number of lanes is taken from the live length of the row.

Above 64 entries the benchmark kernels must not be taken as they are. The block kernel has the right dealing (entry k to thread k mod 256) but merges with cub::BlockReduce; DESIGN.md 2.5 allows library reductions for integers and min/max only, and the host tree is offsets 128, 64, ..., 1. The merge has to be written by hand (for example lane sums in shared memory for offsets 128 to 32, then shuffles in warp 0). From memory, cub::BlockReduce reduces each warp with ascending shuffle offsets and then folds the eight warp results one after another, which would be a different tree; this is not checked here.

The chunk kernels for rows above 8,192 entries cannot reproduce the host order as it is defined today: the host lets each of 256 lanes run over the whole row, and a lane's running compensated sum cannot be cut into chunk results and merged with the same bits. Either the definition in numerics.hpp and the host fold get a chunk rule, or the device folds such a row with one block and n / 256 entries per thread (about 0.5 to 0.6 microseconds per entry per thread, from README_sweeps.md:79-83).

A frontier kernel in lane-group order does not need a new kernel body. A row's lanes and tree depend only on its class and entry positions, so the same light kernel gives identical bits whether it runs over all rows, over a compacted list with a plan built from per-class counts, or over all rows with a flag test. In a flag-test form no thread may leave before the shuffles, because they use the full warp mask.

The price of the old frontier path was its compaction and read-back (34 to 67 microseconds before any kernel work), not the kernel. Stage 1b has to time at least: all rows; flag test inside the full launch; compaction into per-class lists. The chunk kernels already use the flag-test form.

No extra block reduction for the counts: the second cub::BlockReduce pair (block_reduce_counts) and its unconditional use in act_chunk_finalize_kernel are not to be carried over. Integer atomics on a shared-memory counter, used only when the local count is nonzero, are what the owner's rule describes and what the benchmark's A variants do.

A device activity kernel for the real state has to produce more than the benchmark's: per side also the slot of the single infinite entry, the largest finite term and the number of finite terms, with the host's types. The max is a min/max reduction (allowed); the slot sum and term count are integers. Their cost is not in any Stage 0 number, so the 39% and 14% prices and the sweep fits are lower bounds for the real kernel.

The candidate kernel is reusable only as the inner arithmetic (count test, residual first, division). A real one has to add the host rule's tests (side size, error guard from update count and largest term, outward move before integer rounding), the different treatment of continuous columns, comparison with the current bound, infeasibility detection, the marking of changed columns and their rows, and a list of bound changes in a fixed order for the host's postsolve stack.

The device candidate kernel reads one snapshot of bounds and activities for all columns, while the host rule applies each integer bound at once. Equal bounds can be expected only on integer-only models run to an empty frontier, which is what DESIGN.md:698-700 asks the oracle to check; elsewhere each engine is checked for validity.

A frontier-restricted candidate step has no floating-point atomic available for a min or max per column across rows. The column kernel already takes a list of columns, so the form that fits the rules is: flag the columns of the frontier rows (byte stores of the same value), compact them per class, and run the column lane-group kernel over that list.

Contracted operations must stay off in both builds (--fmad=false for device code, -ffp-contract=off for host code) and every fused multiply-add must be an explicit call, as in the benchmark; otherwise the device and the host fold cannot agree in bits.

Not to be used because the result depends on thread timing: the scatter transpose without the segmented sort (scatter_op_t), and the dirty-list kernels with an atomic slot counter (compact_flagged_kernel, emit_frontier_kernel). The hand-back figure of 46 microseconds comes from the latter and does not apply to a deterministic list.

Rebuild: the measured method is CSR compaction followed by a stable radix sort on (column, position), or compaction of the old CSC when entries were only deleted. A real rebuild also has to re-bin rows and columns by length with a stable sort, handle entry tombstones (the benchmark deleted whole rows and columns only), carry the state arrays and the id maps for postsolve, and either keep the 32-bit entry positions with a stated limit below 2^31 nonzeros or widen them.

Memory: every buffer, including CUB temporary storage and pinned buffers, has to come warm from the presolve-owned resource. A fresh device allocation adds about 245 microseconds to a library call and pinned allocation costs 0.38 s per GB. The benchmark's device_vector arrays, its temp_t regrowth and its 110 bytes per nonzero are not a model for the byte budget.

Read-backs are blocking copies in the benchmark (frontier counts, rebuild totals). Each costs about 5 to 14 microseconds and a synchronisation; the real engine should count them in the work estimate, as DESIGN.md 2.1 requires, and avoid them where a fixed launch grid will do.

The thresholds of DESIGN.md 2.1 were derived with the old kernel pair and the old frontier path, on one H200 and one Xeon, with nothing below 71,477 nonzeros and no frontier between 10% and 100% of the rows. They are inputs to the measurements of Stage 1b, not values the device engine can rely on.

The Stage 0 checks are a pattern for tests, not tests: they run once inside the benchmark on plain matrices. The device tests have to be in the gprs test set, use the oracle's MIP models with integer column types where the candidate kernel rounds, compare device activities bit for bit with the host fold (tests/test_state_fold.cpp has the reference), compare frontier rows bit for bit with the full sweep, compare the rebuild with the host, and restore the device memory resource in fixtures.

The PR 2372 regression cases exist as a device check only through a script that is not in the tree. They have to be rebuilt as tests in the project (the host tests already hold the 513-term and 2^54 cases).
open_questions: Rows above 8,192 entries: does the fixed order in numerics.hpp get a chunk rule (host fold changed to match), or does the device fold such rows with one block per row and long per-thread loops? rd-rplusc-21 had a row-side analogue of 119,267 entries in a column and square47 has 1,360 rows above 8,192 with 87.7% of its nonzeros.

Tombstones: the host deals live entries by their rank among the live entries. Will device kernels only ever see rows without tombstones (matrix rebuilt before a device phase, host edits kept in the overlay), or must a device kernel compute live ranks? The benchmark assumes compact rows.

Count type and the flag bit: the owner asks for uint16_t count arrays, the benchmark uses 15 bits plus a 'lo is not zero' flag and saturates at 32,767, the host keeps int32 counts, and DESIGN.md 2.4 says a saturated count marks the row as skipped until recounted and that the error guard, not a flag, decides when lo is loaded. Which of these is the device layout, and how is a saturated row handed between the engines?
The slot of the single infinite entry is a host CSR slot. Is the slot numbering the same on the device (binned storage), or is a map kept, or does the device keep a column id instead?

Count method inside lane groups: the owner's rule names the integer atomic; the measurement shows no difference to carrying the count through the shuffles and a 9% to 11% loss for the atomic on supportcase42. The mixed kernel (shuffles in lane groups, atomic in blocks) was not timed. Is carrying the count through shuffles that exist anyway within the rule?

Bounds layout: the benchmark reads one {lower, upper} pair per column with one load; the host state keeps two arrays, and on Grace Hopper the host is meant to read the mutable state in place. Pairs against two arrays was not measured on the device.
State order on the device: host row and column ids (a scattered write through a map, as measured) or binned order (not measured, needs id translation in the dirty lists)?

Continuous columns: the host records an implied bound with its row and makes it explicit later. Does the device candidate step do the same (it would need the row of the best candidate with a fixed tie rule), or does it tighten only integer columns in Stage 1b?

Is an integer atomic min or max on an order-preserving 64-bit image of a double within the owner's rule? The result does not depend on order, but the rule as worded excludes floating-point atomics; without it a row-driven candidate kernel is not possible.

May the standalone device code depend on rmm (the microbench does, through find_package), or does gprs define its own memory resource with an adapter? And what is the defined behaviour when a device allocation fails, given that nothing may be read from the device and a fall-back to the host engine can change non-integer results?

The deterministic dirty list on a model-sized state is not measured (128 to 135 microseconds on a 1e7-element array only). The analysis notes that a pinned copy of the whole mutable state costs no more than the cheapest list up to about 40,000 rows plus columns; is a whole-state copy below some size acceptable as the fixed-order hand-over?

Column scheduling from 1e6 nonzeros and row scheduling above 1e7 are open in the report (one thread per column up to 64 entries is faster on 7 of 10 matrices between 1e6 and 1e7). The host order now fixes lane groups for row activities at every size; is the candidate kernel's column scheduling free to differ by size, since min and max do not depend on order?

Whether cub::BlockReduce's tree equals the host's 256-lane tree should be checked on the node before any Stage 0 number for rows above 64 entries is reused; I could not read the CUB source on this machine.

constraints_for_design: Lift structure, not arithmetic. calc_act, write_cnst_slack, update_bounds and write_updated_bounds (load_balanced_bounds_presolve_kernels.cuh:42-65, 94-105, 357-422) break every rule of DESIGN.md:280-300: no counters of infinite terms, so the single-infinite column is missed; paired double2 results; side minus activity formed first; no low-order part; no error guard. They have to be replaced by the gprs arithmetic that microbench/sweeps.cu:200-217 and the host engine already use. The live residual-first form (bounds_update_helpers.cuh:196-201) has the right shape but is plain doubles without counters.

The device state must be activities (hi array, separate lo array, two uint16_t count arrays, single-infinite position), not cuOpt's slack pair, because the host engine shares it (state.hpp:86-95). cuOpt's NaN-in-slack flag for an infeasible row must not be copied: a real NaN (for example 0 * infinity) would read as the flag.

Binning must not use cuOpt's atomics (load_balanced_partition_helpers.cuh:104-141): the order inside a bin depends on timing, which breaks the matrix hash and any fixed-order dirty list. DESIGN.md:227 already asks for a stable sort; the bin key formula (32 - clz + popcount > 1) can be kept.

No second copy and 64-bit offsets (DESIGN.md:209, :227-228). cuOpt copies both orientations and uses int offsets; its kernels need the offset type changed and an index scheme decided: cuOpt keeps original ids inside the entries and scatters row results through a map, which the Stage 0 report names as a cost of the benchmark's layout (README_sweeps.md:85-87).

One summation order per row (decision 5) requires that the number of lanes or threads folding a row depends on that row's length class only. cuOpt's small-model path and compact_bins (load_balanced_problem.cu:272-287, 387-390; helpers.cuh:221, 331) make it depend on the longest row of the model and must be dropped or made a tested setting.

Floating-point sums need a tree written in the project and fixed by entry position; cub::BlockReduce::Sum and cub::WarpReduce::Sum on doubles are outside DESIGN.md:304-308. This also applies to the block and chunk kernels of the Stage 0 benchmark (sweeps.cu:251-270). cub and Thrust remain usable for min/max, integer scans, selects and sorts.

Counts of infinite terms: cuOpt has nothing to lift. The rule (count in the scan, one integer atomic when the local count is nonzero) is already implemented in sweeps.cu:354-374 and :393-412 with the atomic on a shared-memory int and one store to the uint16_t array by the group leader or thread 0.

There is no frontier code to lift. The load-balanced loop recomputes everything; the live code's dense flags cost rows + columns per iteration and launch a block per row and column. A frontier kernel in lane-group order needs frontier rows grouped by length class (a list per class or one class-sorted list with a plan), with the same lanes per row as the full sweep. The class lookup by ballot (kernels.cuh:17-40) and the plan of sub_warp_meta (load_balanced_bounds_presolve.cu:92-128) can serve both if the kernel takes an optional row list, as sweeps.cu:359 does.

CUDA graphs can be used in a standalone project unchanged, but cuOpt's graphs are static: arguments and grid sizes are frozen at build time and empty classes are left out. After every re-binning or rebuild the graphs must be rebuilt or their node parameters updated, and a frontier sweep has a grid size that changes every round. The counter read-back should go to pinned memory with an explicit synchronise, not to a pageable class member as in load_balanced_bounds_presolve.cu:351-365.

The chunk length for long lines must be one constant used both for the block count and inside the kernel (cuOpt uses 8,192 and 16,384; helpers.cuh:98 against :163, :628, :716, :1099). Chunk metadata (item id and chunk number per block, segment start per item) is small and can be produced on the host or by a stable device scan; cuOpt's version needs a synchronous read-back.

Loop control must be work based. cuOpt's wall-clock limit changes which bounds are found (load_balanced_bounds_presolve.cu:545-549), its acceptance threshold is 1e3 * absolute tolerance, and its integer rounding has no error-bound test; DESIGN.md sections 2.5 and 6 define other rules.

The lifted kernels assume compact lines with every entry live. Tombstones (index -1), dead rows and removed columns of the gprs state (state.hpp:48-54) would be read as valid ids. Either the device matrix is always compact when a sweep runs, or the kernels test the entry.

Dependencies: raft and every cuOpt header must go; CCCL and rmm may stay (DESIGN.md:584). Replacements: raft::device_span by a pointer-and-length struct or cuda::std::span; raft::handle_t by an explicit stream; raft::copy by cudaMemcpyAsync; raft::ceildiv and raft::WarpSize by constants and integer arithmetic; RAFT_CHECK_CUDA / RAFT_CUDA_TRY by a project check; problem_t views by the gprs device matrix view; tolerances_t and get_cstr_tolerance by the gprs tolerance table; var_t by gprs col_type_t; type_2 / make_span_2 disappear with split arrays; timer_t by the work budget; solver context, solution and probing cache are not lifted.

Device arrays have to come from the presolve-owned memory resource of DESIGN.md:187-205 (managed memory on Grace Hopper, device memory with pinned mirrors on x86). cuOpt allocates everything through rmm::device_uvector on the handle's stream and copies to pageable std::vector (load_balanced_bounds_presolve.cu:141-161); none of that models a host_access / release pair.

cuOpt's parameters are unmeasured variants and fall under the rule that a variant is benchmarked before it replaces another: four entries per lane with at most 16 lanes, block sizes 128 and 1,024 for rows and 64 and 256 for columns, 512 and 640 threads per heavy chunk, ballot dispatch. Stage 0 measured two entries per lane, one 256-thread block size and a loop dispatch, and did not run cuOpt's kernel (STAGE0_REPORT.md:54-55). They fit the Stage 1b item 'other bin boundaries than 64 and 8,192'.

Setup cost: cuOpt launches one 256-thread block per row and per column to copy the matrix (load_balanced_problem.cu:206, :247), builds three graphs and creates 35 streams. With the device matrix built after the first host cascade and rebuilt on the device, the build has to be one pass whose cost does not depend on the number of lines in this way.

Both sweeps should keep cuOpt's property that the activity sweep writes only row results and the bound sweep writes only column bounds, each reading the other's output; this is what makes the result independent of scheduling without any atomic on a floating-point value.

Tests of the bound kernel need integer column types, because the kernel reads the type for rounding (kernels.cuh:437, 496, 537, 585); the regression cases of DESIGN.md:701-702 (x3 <= 5 with one free column, the 2^54 case, the 513-term case) are exactly the cases the lifted arithmetic gets wrong or imprecise.

constraints_for_design: Deliver exactly the six items of the stage table for 1b: memory resource; binned device matrix built after the first host cascade; GPU bound propagation from the lifted load-balanced kernels with lane groups; frontier kernel in the same lane-group order as the full sweep; rebuild (compaction and transpose) on the device; the measurements of the third list, then fixed thresholds. The cuOpt adapter is last and not part of the device engine design.

One summation order per row, identical in the full sweep and the frontier kernel, and defined by entry position in storage order. The host code already defines that order for every engine (lanes = smallest power of two with 2*lanes >= n up to 64 entries, 256 lanes above, entry k to lane k mod lanes, halving-tree merge with dd_add). A device kernel that sums a row from scratch must reproduce it, or the design must say explicitly that it changes the host definition and the stored hashes.

No floating-point atomics anywhere. Infinite-term counts in separate uint16_t arrays (not a paired double), exact, counted in the row scan, one integer atomic only when the thread's local count is nonzero, no extra block reduction for counts; a saturated count marks the row as skipped until recounted. Library reductions only for integers and min/max.

Activities are compensated (hi, lo) sums with error-free products (one explicit fma) and two-sum; a bound change is never applied as a*(new-old); candidates are residual-first; no candidate is emitted when the error bound can exceed the candidate tolerance; contraction off on host (-ffp-contract=off) and device (--fmad=false).

The device propagation must follow the host rule's semantics: no infinite term gives every column a candidate, exactly one only the column that holds it, two or more none; integer columns get the explicit bound tightened and rounded; continuous columns only get an implied bound recorded with its source row and that row's version; the side guard |side| * 1e-14 > feastol and the error guard apply.

Every threshold, budget, pool size and cap is a constant or a function of the model and the settings, with one shipped default; nothing is read from the device except the attribute that selects the memory path, and the memory path must not change any result (the hash sequence is compared across both memory paths).

Every engine threshold must be a settable option so that tests force each path on tiny models: device engine at any size, frontier kernel against full recompute, device rebuild against host rebuild, mirror against gather, managed-memory path against pinned path. The existing pattern is option fields chosen by the seed in the campaign tool.

The device matrix is built after the first host cascade, never on the input. On x86 the hand-over of mutable state uses dirty lists in a fixed record order through pinned buffers and carries bounds, accumulators and counters as bits; the unordered list is not allowed. On Grace Hopper the host reads managed memory in place and that path is functional only, outside the gates, with no time or memory claim.

Device temporaries and pinned buffers come from pools created once; timing is warm (context, pools and pinned buffers exist), cold start is reported separately, and the timed interval runs from the input CSR to the finished reduced model, so device matrix build and uploads are inside it.

Tests required for the device engine: hash sequence after every phase equal across repeated runs and both memory paths (and a second GPU type and thread counts where they exist); a GPU batch equals its sequential replay; frontier kernel bits equal full-sweep bits for the recomputed rows and all other rows untouched; on integer-only models run to an empty frontier host and device engine reach the same bounds; the three PR 2372 cases with integer variable types; fixtures that restore the device memory resource; assertion builds compare a device rebuild against a full recomputation.

Correctness is tested only with the project's oracle and the random campaign tool (tens of millions of models, release and assertion build), plus the structure and crush checks on real instances; no solver-quality test locally. A new check or test must be shown to fail on a deliberately wrong kernel.

Every kernel variant is benchmarked against the current one before it replaces it; scheduling choices that the plan leaves open (rows above 1e7 nonzeros, columns from 1e6, bin boundaries other than 64 and 8,192, layout in place, split against paired arrays, loading lo on demand) are settled by Stage 1b measurements, not by assumption.

The host-only build must stay free of CUDA: no device source may be a .cpp file directly in gpu_presolve/src, gpu_presolve/tests or gpu_presolve/tools (four globs and the Mac script compile those), and no header reachable from presolve.hpp, state.hpp, rules.hpp or numerics.hpp may include CUDA or rmm headers. The Mac has neither CMake nor CUDA, so build_host_local.sh must keep passing unchanged.

Inferred layout that fits the existing conventions: device sources and tests in their own subdirectories or with .cu/.cuh extensions, built by a CUDA target that links gprs_host (either an option in the top-level CMakeLists that is off by default or a separate project directory like microbench/ and check/), with find_package(rmm), --fmad=false -Xcompiler=-ffp-contract=off, an assertion and a release build, and a sequential replay of each kernel in plain C++ that also compiles on the Mac so that the replay comparison and most logic can be tested without a GPU.

The run identity (tools/run_info.py SOURCE_PATHS) must cover the device sources, and a device run driver should follow stage1_host_runs.sh: builds and data on the scratch, step markers keyed on the source identity, restartable, the same lock as the host timed runs so that device runs and single-core timings never overlap, results under gpu_presolve/results/stage1/<device directory>/<tag>.

The standalone project must not include any cuOpt header or target; the load-balanced kernels, partition helpers, graph builders and bounds-update helpers are lifted once as copies and rewritten for compensated sums and counters (the originals use plain sums, recompute every row and have no infinity counters).

Gates that the default configuration must still pass once the device engine is on from 5e5 nonzeros: per-instance time rule on the minimum of three alternating runs, band geomean and median, reductions geomean at least 0.99 with every instance below 0.95 explained, row dynamism limit; FAILED is an assertion. Per the relayed user message, removing more than the HiGHS reference is the aim and must not count as a gate failure.
Device-detected fixings and infeasibility must reach the host in a deterministic order, because fixings create postsolve records and the postsolve hash covers the records in order.

Project rules from the user's memory that apply: the design is agreed in chat before any edit, build or run of a new framework; dev-node tests stay small (minutes); each milestone is committed and pushed on feat/gpu-presolve; a HISTORY.md entry is appended every session; working data on the scratch because the node can drop.
open_questions: Rows above 8,192 entries: the host definition (numerics.hpp:139-155) uses 256 lanes whatever the row length, DESIGN.md 2.3 (lines 224-225) stores them as chunks, DESIGN.md 2.4 (lines 261-263) says a longer row is folded by one block, and the Stage 0 benchmark summed per chunk and then over the partial results. Which is it? One 256-lane block over the whole row keeps the host bits but is not load-balanced; a chunk scheme needs a new order on the host as well, which changes the stored hashes of the instances with such rows (5 of 32 matrices).

Is bit equality between a device from-scratch sum and the host fold_row_activity required, or only frontier kernel against full sweep on the device? The plan's tests demand only the second; the host header says the order is the same in every engine. The answer decides whether the device may use cub::BlockReduce (whose tree differs from the host's halving tree) and whether the decision 5 fallback (one thread per row up to 64) must emulate the lane order.

The host order is defined over the live entries of a row (k-th live entry to lane k mod lanes) and the lane count depends on the current live length. The device matrix has entry tombstones and bins that are rebuilt only at a rebuild. How does a device kernel sum a row with tombstones, or a row whose live length crossed a class boundary since the last binning? (Inferred options: only compact rows on the device, or re-bin before a sweep.)

Who owns the matrix in Stage 1b? DESIGN.md 2.2 describes a device-primary matrix with an optional pinned mirror and a copy-on-write row overlay for host edits; the Stage 1a state_t owns the whole matrix in std::vector storage and every Stage 1 rule edits it in place. How do host row edits reach the device before a device propagation, and does the 'no mirror above 64 MiB, gather on demand' case exist at all while all rules run on the host state?

Must state_t's arrays move into the presolve-owned memory resource (pinned or managed allocations) for the Grace Hopper path and for pinned hand-overs? They are std::vector members today (state.hpp:62-69, 212-243), and the header is listed as a fixed shared interface.

Does 'rebuild on the device' in Stage 1b have to reproduce state_t::rebuild() exactly (order of live entries kept, fixed-column terms folded into the sides as one compensated sum, activities of rows that lost a slot recomputed, inf_slot shifted) and write the result back into the host state, or is the device rebuild only a re-upload and re-binning of what the host rebuilt? The plan says the engine is chosen by the work estimate but not what a device rebuild returns to the host.

On the device, are activities of changed rows always recomputed from scratch (what the frontier-kernel test and the lifted kernels imply), or also updated incrementally by two terms as on the host? The user's first feedback asked for compensated sums instead of recomputation from scratch (HISTORY.md:100-101); the plan does not say which the device does.

The error guard: the plan's bound n*u^2*T is known not to be a bound (HISTORY.md:943-946; state.hpp:415-419). Which formula does the device guard use, and is it the same expression as on the host so that both engines suppress the same candidates on integer-only models?

The plan loads lo only when hi alone cannot pass the guard (DESIGN.md:297-299), but the host pair is not normalised and hi can be 0 while lo holds the value (state.hpp:84-85). Is the pair normalised on the device, is a nonzero-lo flag kept as in the Stage 0 benchmark (bit 15 of the count, which caps the count at 32767), or is lo always loaded?

Device counts are uint16_t with saturation; the host has int32 counts, an int64 slot sum for the position of the single infinite entry, and per side max_term and updates. What is the record format of the hand-over, how is a saturated row represented on the host, and in which numbering is the single-infinite position stored when the device matrix is binned and the host slots are not?

Decision 5 says the fallback is taken if the lane-group frontier kernel 'is slow'. Against what, and by how much? The same holds for fixing the thresholds: the plan gives no objective (for example never slower than the host engine beyond the 12 to 15% run noise) and no rule for instances where the wrong engine is chosen.

Does the 5e5 default apply to the input size or to the size after the first host cascade, and do the 32,000 and 100,000 thresholds apply to the current model as it shrinks? The duty to measure 20,000 to 70,000 nonzeros suggests the current size, but the plan does not say.

Two rules decide between a frontier-restricted sweep and recomputing all rows: a share of the nonzeros held by the affected rows (DESIGN.md:270-272) and '1e6 nonzeros and at most 1% of the rows' (DESIGN.md:174). Which form does the final threshold take?

Lane groups are decided only for bands A and B, while the device engine is on by default only from 5e5 nonzeros, so by default the fixed row rule covers band B alone and bands C and D (where lane groups were 1.14 times slower) have no rule. Must Stage 1b settle the rule above 1e7 nonzeros before any default is fixed?

Hash comparison across 'thread counts' and 'early heuristics on and off': the standalone host engine is sequential and early heuristics exist only in cuOpt. Do these two dimensions wait for the adapter? Is a second GPU type available on the dev node or the cluster, and is a GH200 node available (open item 1 of the plan)?

Phase hashes with a device-resident state: the hash is computed on the host state, so every phase needs the state on the host when phase_hashes is on. Is a download at every phase acceptable in that mode, and how many hash entries does a cascade that alternates between engines produce (the host sequence is fixed at one per phase)?

'Both engines reach the same bounds on integer-only models run to an empty frontier' does not say what happens when a budget, the pass cap, the error guard or a detected infeasibility stops one engine first. Is the test restricted to models where neither engine stops early, with unlimited budgets?

'A GPU batch equals its sequential replay' is not defined for a propagation sweep. My reading: all candidates are computed on the state at the start of the sweep and merged per column by min/max, and the replay does the same on the host in a loop. For the implied-bound record of a continuous column the winning source row on equal candidates needs a fixed tie rule (smallest row index?).

Warm timing needs the context, pools and pinned buffers to exist before the timed call, but run_engine.py starts one gprs_presolve process per repetition. Should the device tool warm up in-process (untimed first call or explicit pool creation) and report cold start apart?

Stored results show the propagation family is about 7% of the host engine's time and is called 1 to 9 times per presolve on almost every instance. Is it accepted that Stage 1b cannot improve the Stage 1 time gate noticeably and that its purpose is the infrastructure and the thresholds for Stage 2, with the default device threshold possibly ending above every testbed size?

Where should device code live: an option in the top-level CMakeLists (off by default) with sources in subdirectories, or a separate project directory in the style of microbench/ and check/? Section 11 of the plan describes one static library with CUDA as a dependency, which the host-only Stage 1a build does not follow.

What I read myself, beyond the four reader reports: include/gprs/numerics.hpp, state.hpp, rules.hpp, presolve.hpp; src/rules_propagation.cpp, rules_bounds.cpp, state_ops.cpp, presolve.cpp in full; src/state_build.cpp lines 60-350, state_storage.cpp lines 1-220, hash.cpp lines 100-211; DESIGN.md lines 27-447 and 581-704; microbench/sweeps.cu lines 96-770; check/CMakeLists.txt; the head of tools/run_info.py, tools/gprs_fuzz.cpp lines 200-260 and the head of tests/oracle.hpp (all under /Users/acoerduek/Documents/workspace/cuopt-wt/gpu-presolve/gpu_presolve or .../design_summaries/gpu_mip_presolve). Cost figures are the Stage 0 figures as the readers quote them. Three statements are from memory and marked as such where used: that nvcc accepts std::fma in a host-and-device function, that CUB select and radix sort keep order, and the name of the CUDA device attribute for direct managed-memory access.

The design in eight sentences.
1. The host state stays the only authority. The device engine is a function from (current matrix, bounds, frontier rows) to an ordered list of bound changes, implied-bound candidates and an outcome; its result enters the host state only through the existing host operations tighten_lower, tighten_upper and record_implied_lower/upper, in ascending column order. Every state invariant, list, counter, postsolve record and the objective offset then hold by construction, and state_hash and consistency_error work unchanged at every phase end.
2. The device never updates an activity incrementally. Every activity it uses is a fold from scratch in the order of numerics.hpp:139-155, so a device candidate is, bit for bit, the value the host function candidate() returns on a row that recompute_row_activity has just summed. The validity argument of the host rule applies without a new case, and frontier bits equal full-sweep bits because both are the same function of the same inputs.
3. The semantics are defined once, in plain C++ in the host tree (a reference backend that also builds on the Mac). The CUDA backend must equal it bit for bit, round by round. This is the test "a GPU batch equals its sequential replay".
4. Two sweeps as in cuOpt's load-balanced code: rows are folded over the binned CSR, candidates are reduced per column over the binned CSC by min/max. No floating-point atomic and no library reduction on a sum is used; each sweep writes only what the other reads.
5. Rows up to 64 entries use the Stage 0 lane-group kernel (it already has the host tree); longer rows use one 256-thread block per row with a hand-written tree with offsets 128 to 1, also above 8,192 entries, so numerics.hpp and the stored host hashes do not change.
6. The device matrix is a canonical binned copy of the live host matrix. It is re-derived when the host changed entries (no overlay in Stage 1b) and compacted on the device when the host only deleted; both give the same arrays.
7. All scheduling choices (full sweep, flag test, per-class lists; whole-array upload or scattered records; device compaction or re-upload; memory path) are made result-neutral, so only four thresholds can change a result and the hash sequence.
8. Milestones: M0 semantics and protocol on the host with the reference backend, M1 memory resource and device arithmetic, M2 binned matrix and folds, M3 device propagation, M4 frontier forms, M5 device rebuild, M6 measurements, M7 fixed thresholds.

What the safety measures cost (details in the other fields): hand-back by host replay costs the CSC length of the changed columns on the host (about 10 to 20 ns per entry, to be measured) instead of one write per changed row; the sync by counters and mirror comparison costs time proportional to rows plus columns per device call; column-driven candidates read every entry of each candidate column, not only the frontier entries; one block per row above 8,192 entries has a latency of n/256 entries per thread (about 0.26 ms for the 119,267-entry line of rd-rplusc-21, from 0.5 to 0.6 microseconds per entry); any entry edit by a host rule forces a re-upload of the matrix (about 2 to 3 ns per nonzero on the host, estimated). Stored results show bound propagation is about 7% of the host engine's time, so Stage 1b is not expected to move the Stage 1 time gate; its value is the tested infrastructure and the measured thresholds.
decisions_for_owner: Hand-back. DESIGN.md 2.2 says the dirty lists carry bounds, accumulators and counters as bits. This design hands back only bound changes and implied-bound candidates and lets the host replay them through tighten_lower / tighten_upper; device accumulators never reach the host. It is the safer form (all invariants by construction) and costs the CSC length of the changed columns on the host. Is this deviation from 2.2 accepted for Stage 1b, with the bit hand-back kept as a variant to measure?

Scope of 'rebuild on the device'. Here it rebuilds the device's binned matrix (compaction, re-binning, transpose) and is tested equal to a build from the rebuilt host state; state_t::rebuild stays on the host. Replacing the host rebuild pays only if state_t's arrays live in the presolve memory resource (pinned or managed), because a download into std::vector storage costs about as much as the host rebuild (40 bytes per nonzero; estimated). That means changing the array types in state.hpp. In Stage 1b, or with the overlay design before Stage 2?

Is an integer atomic minimum or maximum on an order-preserving 64-bit image of a double within 'no floating-point atomics'? Its result does not depend on order. It would allow a row-driven candidate step whose work is the frontier nonzeros instead of the full length of the candidate columns. The baseline does not need it.

Which machine serves as the second GPU type for the hash comparison, and is a GH200 node available (open item 1 of the plan)? Without them both checks stay at 'same GPU type' and 'managed path forced on x86'.

When the device engine cannot get its memory (need above the byte budget, or an allocation fails): this design makes the first a deterministic 'not eligible' and the second a hard error. Inside cuOpt, should a failed allocation instead rerun the presolve on the host, which gives a result that differs from other machines?

If M6 shows no model size at which device propagation beats the host by more than the noise: ship min_nnz as 'never' (device propagation off by default, infrastructure kept for Stage 2), or keep the plan's 5e5 default at a known cost?
